sections.title: Structure determines function
sections.text:
Materials science connects internal structure with useful properties. The same chemical element can form materials with different behaviour when its bonding or arrangement changes. Crystal structure, grain boundaries, impurities, porosity and processing influence strength, conductivity and corrosion resistance. Selecting a material therefore requires more than memorizing its chemical name.

Ceramics are mainly inorganic non-metallic materials produced or consolidated through appropriate processing. Many are hard, heat resistant and chemically stable but brittle because cracks can grow without much plastic deformation. Examples include porcelain, bricks, alumina components and specialized electronic ceramics. Glass is commonly amorphous rather than an ordinary ordered crystal. Neither “all ceramics are insulators” nor “all ceramics are fragile under every loading condition” is universally correct.

Composites combine distinct materials to obtain useful properties. Reinforced concrete joins concrete's compressive strength with reinforcement that carries tension. Fibre-reinforced polymers combine strong fibres with a binding matrix. Performance depends on bonding between components as well as their individual properties.

sections.title: Plastics, polymers and environmental behaviour
sections.text:
A polymer is a large molecule formed from repeating or related building units. Polyethylene consists of long chains derived from ethylene. Chain length, branching, crystallinity and additives affect flexibility and strength. Plastics are formulated polymer materials, often containing fillers, pigments, stabilizers or plasticizers.

Thermoplastics soften and can often be reshaped on heating because their chains can move relative to one another. Thermosetting plastics form extensive cross-links during curing and do not normally remelt into a flowing liquid; strong heating may degrade them. Elastomers are polymers capable of large reversible deformation within their working conditions.

| Category | Structural feature | Typical application |
|---|---|---|
| Thermoplastic | Chains can move when sufficiently heated | Containers, pipes and packaging |
| Thermoset | Cross-linked network | Heat-resistant electrical parts and adhesives |
| Elastomer | Flexible network with elastic recovery | Seals and tyres |

Recyclability depends on polymer type, contamination, additives and collection systems. “Biobased” means the feedstock has a biological origin; “biodegradable” concerns breakdown under specified environmental conditions. A biobased plastic is not automatically biodegradable, and an industrially compostable product may persist in seawater or an open dump. Microplastics are small plastic particles produced through fragmentation or manufactured at small sizes. Their behaviour depends on size, chemistry and environmental conditions.

sections.title: Semiconductors and electronic devices
sections.text:
Semiconductors have electronic structures that permit controllable charge transport. Silicon's conductivity can be changed by doping, the introduction of selected impurities. Donor dopants produce n-type material with electrons as majority carriers; acceptor dopants produce p-type material with holes as majority carriers. A hole describes the mobile absence of an electron in a filled band, not a free proton travelling through the crystal.

At a p–n junction, carriers diffuse and leave a depletion region containing fixed ionized dopants. An internal electric field develops. Forward bias reduces the barrier and permits substantial conduction under suitable conditions; reverse bias generally widens depletion and limits current until regimes such as breakdown occur. This asymmetry supports rectification.

Transistors control electrical current and can function as switches or amplifiers. Integrated circuits combine many devices on a chip. Solar cells and LEDs also rely on semiconductor physics, but their purposes differ: solar cells convert incoming light to electrical power; LEDs convert electrical input to emitted light. Semiconductor conductivity also responds to temperature and illumination, so these materials are useful in sensors.

sections.title: Fertilizers and soil fertility
sections.text:
Plants require mineral nutrients for growth. Nitrogen supports proteins and nucleic acids, phosphorus participates in ATP and nucleic acids, and potassium helps regulate enzyme activity and cellular water relations. Fertilizers supply selected nutrients; they do not replace adequate water, light, healthy roots or appropriate soil conditions.

Nitrogen fertilizers include urea and ammonium-based products; phosphate and potassium fertilizers supply other major nutrients. Organic amendments can add nutrients and improve soil properties, but nutrient release depends on decomposition. Soil testing, crop needs, timing and application placement help determine suitable use. More fertilizer does not guarantee more yield once another factor becomes limiting.

Nutrients lost through runoff or leaching can pollute water. Nitrate is relatively mobile in many soils, while phosphorus often travels with eroded sediment or dissolved runoff. Excess fertilizer can also harm crops through salt effects. Integrated nutrient management combines appropriate mineral and organic sources with soil conservation and efficient irrigation.

sections.title: Pesticides and integrated pest management
sections.text:
Pesticides control organisms considered harmful in a particular setting. Insecticides target insects, herbicides weeds and fungicides fungal diseases. Selectivity varies: a product intended for one pest may affect beneficial organisms, aquatic life or humans if exposure occurs. Toxicity describes inherent harmful potential; risk also depends on dose and exposure.

Repeated use of one mode of action can select resistant pest populations. Resistance develops in organisms rather than because the chemical becomes “used to” the crop. Integrated pest management combines monitoring, action thresholds, crop practices, biological controls and carefully selected chemical use. Its purpose is to manage damage while reducing unnecessary pesticide dependence.

Persistent chemicals can remain in soil and sediment, and some accumulate in food webs. Safe storage, application controls, residue monitoring and container management matter throughout the pesticide lifecycle. Antibiotics and vaccines are also prescribed in the physical-science syllabus's chemical applications, but their biological mechanisms and public-health significance are developed together in Chapter 13 to avoid duplicating the explanation.

**Materials in a device lifecycle.** A semiconductor device needs not only an active crystal but also conductors, insulating layers, packaging and thermal management. Ceramics may provide electrical insulation or specialized electronic functions; polymers protect components; metals carry current and remove heat. The useful product is a coordinated assembly. Recycling it can be difficult because small quantities of many materials are tightly integrated, explaining why electronic waste requires more careful handling than ordinary packaging waste.

**Fertilizer response and limiting factors.** A crop with insufficient nitrogen may respond to nitrogen fertilizer, but further addition gives little benefit when water, phosphorus or another factor limits growth. Soil texture and organic matter influence retention, while timing determines whether roots can use the nutrient before it is lost. The same nutrient amount can therefore produce different outcomes under different management. Appropriate application reduces losses without assuming that all mineral fertilizer is harmful or all organic material is automatically safe.

**Pest control as an ecological decision.** Natural enemies, crop rotation, resistant varieties and physical barriers can reduce pest pressure. Monitoring distinguishes an economically important pest population from a harmless presence. Chemical treatment should address a relevant target and mode of action rather than eliminate all visible insects. Beneficial pollinators and predators can be harmed by poorly chosen controls, sometimes creating additional pest problems. Integrated management follows evidence about the whole crop system.

questions.prompt: A cross-linked thermosetting polymer is reheated after curing. Why does it usually not remelt and flow like an ordinary thermoplastic?

options.B: It is always a metallic conductor
options.D: A covalent network restricts ordinary chain flow and may degrade before melting

questions.explanation: Extensive cross-linking prevents normal thermoplastic melting and flow.

questions.prompt: Adding suitable donor impurities to silicon typically produces an n-type semiconductor whose majority mobile carriers are:
questions.explanation: Donor dopants contribute electrons to conduction under suitable conditions, so electrons become majority carriers.

questions.prompt: Applying increasing reverse bias to an ordinary p–n junction typically causes its depletion region to:
questions.explanation: Reverse bias increases the junction's potential barrier and generally widens the depletion region until other regimes, such as breakdown, become relevant.
